passage:
You want to know if my friends ever had it hard? Listen to your Vidya Nani. This was 1998, in Hyderabad. My friend Raghav fell for Shaheen from our college, and I watched the whole thing.
First it was small things. Raghav learning to eat haleem without making a face. Shaheen learning our gang's silly nicknames. Her friends teasing him about cricket; ours teasing her about her poetry.
Then, only four months in, his mother asked the question: "And what will the children be?" Her abba asked where they would live, and whose festivals they would keep.
What I remember is this: Raghav didn't hide behind Shaheen, and she didn't hide behind him. They went to both houses together. They said, "We don't know every answer yet, but we'll decide as a pair." Not everyone was happy. But I knew then they could stand together outside, not just in the canteen.

qa.q: What did Raghav's mother ask?
qa.a: His mother asked, 'And what will the children be?'

qa.q: What did Vidya believe about the couple after they visited both houses together?
qa.a: Vidya felt confident that Raghav and Shaheen could face the outside world together, since neither hid behind the other.

qa.q: What did Raghav and Shaheen do well when the family questions came?
qa.a: They went to both houses together and answered as a pair, admitting they didn't know every answer but would decide jointly.

qa.q: How might Shaheen's abba have felt asking where they'd live?
qa.a: Her abba was probably worried about her future and traditions, and asking was his way of checking whether the couple had thought it through.

grounding: Shows a friend watching a young couple adjust to each other's food and friends and face early family questions about religion and household together.

passage:
The power went at noon on Eid, just as Rehana's family sat down to lunch in their Kozhikode flat, and the fans slowed to nothing. Jyoti, there as Rehana's college friend, watched Faraz from Lucknow sweat through his new kurta and still reach for a second helping of pathiri.
"He's learning," Rehana whispered. Two months ago he'd called Malabar biryani "too mild".
Rehana's aunt fanned herself with a plate. "So Faraz, after marriage you'll take her to Lucknow? Joint family?"
The room went quiet except for the traffic outside.
Faraz glanced at Rehana. She gave a small nod. "We've talked about it, Khala," he said. "We'd like to start on our own, near both our jobs, and visit both families often. We're still working out the details together."
The aunt raised an eyebrow. Rehana squeezed his hand under the table. Jyoti thought: they rehearsed this, and they did it side by side.

qa.q: What did Faraz reach for a second helping of?
qa.a: Faraz reached for a second helping of pathiri.

qa.q: What did Jyoti think when Faraz answered the aunt?
qa.a: Jyoti felt impressed, thinking the couple had rehearsed the answer and faced the question side by side.

qa.q: What helped Faraz and Rehana handle the aunt's question?
qa.a: They had already discussed where to live, checked with each other through a glance and a nod, and gave one shared answer instead of leaving one person to defend it.

qa.q: How might Rehana's aunt see Faraz after this lunch?
qa.a: The aunt may still have doubts, as her raised eyebrow shows, but she has seen Faraz answer respectfully and speak for both of them.

grounding: Illustrates a friend observing a couple adjusting to each other's food and family, and facing an early question about their future household together.

passage:
Suraj had known Chinmay since school, so he noticed every small change once Chinmay started dating Fatima.

At first it was little things. Chinmay, who used to eat anything, learned to order the vegetarian thali when they all went out, because Fatima didn't eat pork and he'd decided to make meals simpler for everyone. Fatima started coming to their Sunday cricket and cheering badly.

Then, one evening at Suraj's flat, Chinmay went quiet over dinner. "Mom asked me yesterday what Fatima's 'community' is. Just like that."

Fatima put down her spoon. "My father asked the same thing about you last week."

They looked at each other across the table. Suraj waited for someone to change the subject.

Instead Fatima said, "So we tell them together. Not separately." Chinmay nodded slowly.

Suraj realised they weren't just a couple anymore. They were a team facing something.

qa.q: What did Chinmay's mom ask him?
qa.a: What Fatima's "community" is.

qa.q: How does Suraj feel when Chinmay and Fatima look at each other across the table?
qa.a: Suraj feels a little tense and uncertain, waiting for someone to change the subject, and then quietly impressed that they face it together.

qa.q: What choice did Chinmay and Fatima make, and why does it matter?
qa.a: They decided to tell their families together, not separately, which tests and strengthens whether they can face the outside as a couple.

qa.q: What might it be like for Fatima to hear Chinmay's mother's question?
qa.a: She may feel hurt and wary, recognising the same worry her own father has, but also determined not to let it split them.

grounding: Suraj, a friend, watches Chinmay and Fatima adjust to each other's worlds and face family questions about community together early on.

passage:
"Deepak, since when do you eat karela?"

"Since Sunita's mother made it for me, Hemant. Three times."

"And you ate it?"

"I finished it. I said it was the best thing I'd eaten."

"You hate karela."

"I know. But her mother was watching me like an exam."

"Ha. How did the rest go?"

"Her father asked about my family. What my father does. Where we're from. Then, very politely, our surname."

"Ah. The surname question."

"Sunita squeezed my hand under the table. After, she told me her father would ask more. She said, 'Whatever they ask, we answer together.'"

"And your side?"

"My mother keeps saying 'these things matter later.' I told her Sunita is coming for Pongal."

"Okay. You two are serious."

"We are. Pass the chips. I need to recover from the karela."

qa.q: Who made karela for Deepak?
qa.a: Sunita's mother.

qa.q: What does Deepak's finishing the karela show about how he felt?
qa.a: It shows he was nervous and eager to please, feeling watched and tested by Sunita's mother.

qa.q: How can Deepak and Sunita handle their families' questions well?
qa.a: By answering together, as Sunita said, and being honest with both families rather than letting either side decide for them.

qa.q: How does Hemant see Deepak and Sunita now?
qa.a: Hemant, as a friend, sees they have become serious, moving from dating to facing family expectations together.

grounding: Hemant, a friend, hears how Deepak adjusts to Sunita's family food and questions about surname, showing the couple learning to face families together.

passage:
I've shared a room with Akash since first year, so I've had a front-row seat to him and Rosy.

The first few months were all late-night calls and inside jokes. Then came the food. Rosy's family is Syrian Christian from Kottayam; they eat beef at Christmas. Akash's family is strict vegetarian. The first time Rosy came to our room with a tiffin of her mother's cutlets, Akash asked, very carefully, what was in them. She laughed and said, "Chicken, don't worry."

Last week Akash came back from home looking grey. His father had asked, "What will you two do about religion? About children?" Akash hadn't known what to say.

That night I heard him on the phone with Rosy for two hours. At the end he said, "We'll figure it out. Both of us. Not me alone."

I don't know how it'll turn out. But they're facing it together.

— Karthik

qa.q: What was in the cutlets Rosy brought?
qa.a: Chicken.

qa.q: How does Karthik feel watching Akash and Rosy?
qa.a: Karthik feels concerned but hopeful, unsure how it will turn out but moved that they are facing it together.

qa.q: What could help Akash and Rosy at this stage?
qa.a: Talking openly with each other and then with both families, facing the questions as a team rather than alone.

qa.q: What is it like for Akash to hear his father ask about religion and children?
qa.a: He feels shaken and unprepared, which is why he came back looking grey.

grounding: Karthik, a roommate, observes Akash and Rosy adjusting to different food and family expectations, with religion raised early and faced together.

passage: Coach's notebook, Thursday. Uma and Vijay stayed back after rehearsal again, and I overheard more than I meant to. Last Sunday Uma ate lunch at Vijay's home for the first time. She told me she had practised eating fish curry with her fingers so nobody would think her fussy, and that his cousins teased her Tamil accent kindly. This week it was Vijay's turn: he sat through her grandmother's questions about his surname and his family's church. What struck me was not the questions but how the two of them answered. When Uma's aunt asked, "And where will you live, whose festivals will you keep?", Vijay looked at Uma before replying, and she said, "We are still working that out together." Both looked tired tonight. I told them the green room is free on Fridays if they want a quiet place to talk, and I will keep checking in.

qa.q: What did Uma practise before lunch at Vijay's home?
qa.a: She practised eating fish curry with her fingers so nobody would think her fussy.

qa.q: What does the coach seem to feel while watching Uma and Vijay after rehearsal?
qa.a: The coach seems concerned about how tired they look and also impressed by how they answer the family's questions as a pair.

qa.q: What support could help the couple at this stage of meeting families?
qa.a: A quiet place to agree on their answers in private, like the green room the coach offered, helps them face questions about home and festivals as a team.

qa.q: What is it like for Vijay when Uma's grandmother asks about his surname and his family's church?
qa.a: It is probably tense and exposing to be judged on his background, though looking to Uma before replying shows he wants them to answer together.

grounding: Shows an onlooker noticing a young couple adjusting to each other's food, families and questions of faith and household, and facing them together.
